items.prompt: Which of these is a key result?
choices: Make the service feel more dependable to everyone using it
P1 incidents drop from 8 per quarter to 2 or fewer
Become known as a reliable team across the whole company
items.explanation: A key result is a number that either moved or did not. The other two are qualitative.

items.prompt: What does an objective mainly answer?
choices: Why does this matter?
Did it happen by Friday?
Who is on call?
items.explanation: An objective is the qualitative, motivating statement of why the work matters.

items.prompt: What does a key result mainly answer?
choices: Why does this matter to us?
Did it actually happen?
Who approved the plan?
items.explanation: A key result is measurable and falsifiable: it either happened or it did not.

items.prompt: What does OKR stand for?
choices: Outcomes and Key Reports
Objectives and Known Risks
Objectives and Key Results
items.explanation: OKR is the shorthand for an objective paired with the key results that measure it.

items.prompt: Why is 'improve code quality' weak as a goal?
choices: The phrase is too short to be read properly
Nobody can tell whether it happened
Quality improvements are never worth the effort
items.explanation: It defines no number, so the end-of-quarter verdict becomes an argument.

items.prompt: Which is the best key result for the objective 'faster support'?
choices: Support staff try hard to answer faster this quarter
Replies feel quicker to customers who write in
Median first reply drops from 6 hours to 2
items.explanation: The third states a measurable change. The numbers are a hypothetical illustration.

items.prompt: An objective with no key results is closest to a...
choices: Support staff try to go faster
Replies feel quicker to customers
Median first reply drops from 6 hours to 2
items.explanation: Without measurable results, an objective is a motivating phrase nobody can check.

items.prompt: Key results with no objective are closest to...
choices: a promise that nobody ever actually made
a spreadsheet nobody is inspired by
a slogan with no message behind it
items.explanation: Numbers with no stated purpose are measurable but give nobody a reason to care.

items.prompt: What is a cascading goal?
choices: One picked from the team's own wish list
One copied word for word from the company plan
One derived from what the level above needs
items.explanation: A cascading goal is a genuine contribution to what the level above needs.

items.prompt: What should a manager ask first when setting a team goal?
choices: What does the organization need from us now?
What would be quickest to finish?
What did we enjoy the most about last quarter?
items.explanation: Starting from organizational need keeps the goal aimed at the right problem.

items.prompt: The team worked hard but outages stayed the same. What does this show?
choices: The team should have simply worked longer hours
Effort alone does not prove the goal was right
Outages cannot be reduced by any team at all
items.explanation: Effort and aim are separate. Hard work on the wrong target still misses the need.

items.prompt: Leadership judges a quarter mainly by...
choices: how busy the team looked
how many tasks were closed
whether the real problem moved
items.explanation: What counts is whether the organization's actual problem changed.

items.prompt: A number is added: 'raise test coverage by 10 points'. Does that fix the missing link?
choices: No, checkable is not the same as right
Yes, any number at all fixes the goal
Yes, so long as the number is ambitious
items.explanation: A number makes a goal checkable. Only tracing it upward makes it the right goal.

items.prompt: Which goal traces to the priority of saving an outage-driven renewal?
choices: Refresh the design of the team wiki pages
Reduce severe production incidents
Hold more team social events this quarter
items.explanation: Reducing severe incidents addresses the outages behind the renewal risk.

items.prompt: Must a team goal always trace to a company need?
choices: Only goals about customers must trace
Yes, though it may take several hops
No, team goals stand apart from company ones
items.explanation: The chain can have several hops, but it should exist and be explainable.

items.prompt: Can a goal be fully accomplished and still be the wrong goal?
choices: No, finishing proves it was right
Only if it was far too easy for the team
Yes, if it was never tied to a need
items.explanation: A goal tied to no real need can be completed without helping anyone.

items.prompt: How many tests must a goal pass here?
choices: Two: a number and a link upward
One: only the number test
Three, including team morale and budget
items.explanation: The two tests are measurability and traceability.

items.prompt: Test one asks...
choices: Who will approve the budget for the goal?
What number will tell us this happened?
How long did the last goal take to finish?
items.explanation: The first test checks that the goal has a measurable result.

items.prompt: Test two asks...
choices: How many people can be assigned to work on it?
Which tool will we use to track its progress?
What does it connect to one level up?
items.explanation: The second test checks the link to what the level above needs.

items.prompt: A goal has a number but no link to organizational need. It...
choices: fails the second test
passes both
fails the first test of the two
items.explanation: The number satisfies test one, but the missing upward link fails test two.

items.prompt: A goal is tied to a priority but has no number. It...
choices: fails the first test
fails the second test
passes both tests
items.explanation: The link satisfies test two, but nothing measurable fails test one.

items.prompt: In incident terms, what does P1 mean?
choices: A low-severity cosmetic bug
The first release of the quarter
The highest-severity incident tier
items.explanation: P1 is the top severity tier, the kind that can threaten a renewal.

items.prompt: Does the chain to a company need have to be one hop?
choices: Yes, only one single hop is acceptable
No, it must exist and be explainable
Yes, more than two hops always fails
items.explanation: Several hops are fine as long as the chain can be explained.

items.prompt: Does the two-question test apply outside engineering?
choices: Only to sales teams
No, only to outage goals
Yes, to any team's goal
items.explanation: Support, design and sales goals can fail the same two ways.

items.prompt: What is a skill gap analysis?
choices: Ranking every teammate by their past performance
Comparing current ability with what the goal needs
Counting the free hours each person has this quarter
items.explanation: It identifies the difference between current ability and the goal's requirements.

items.prompt: When should the gap be named?
choices: Up front, in the plan
At the quarter review
Only if the goal fails
items.explanation: Naming it early lets the plan account for learning and support.

items.prompt: Nobody has written a runbook, yet the key result needs ten. What is the risk?
choices: Ten rough documents that nobody trusts
The team writes too quickly
Leadership asks for fewer key results to track
items.explanation: Without the skill, the key result may be met on paper but fail in real use.

items.prompt: What can a plan do once a gap is named?
choices: Ignore the gap and trust the effort alone
Lower every other target quietly instead
Pair the first attempt with an expert
items.explanation: Pairing and review are ways to close the gap during the quarter.

items.prompt: A runbook nobody trusts during an incident has...
choices: met the letter but not the need
fully delivered the key result
made the outage impossible to repeat
items.explanation: The document exists, but the reason for the key result was not met.

items.prompt: The skill gap is the distance between...
choices: two quarters' budgets compared side by side
how many meetings the team holds each week
current ability and what the goal needs
items.explanation: That distance is what the plan has to cover.

items.prompt: An unnamed gap usually leads to...
choices: a bigger budget that gets approved on its own
a key result missed or met only on paper
faster delivery thanks to the added pressure
items.explanation: Silent assumptions of skill the team lacks cause quiet failure.

items.prompt: Which of these is a skill gap?
choices: The team has never written incident runbooks
The team likes the tools it currently uses
The office is moving to a different floor soon
items.explanation: A skill gap is something the goal requires that the team cannot yet do.

items.prompt: The three questions are measurable, within the team's control, and...
choices: traces to the objective
has a catchy name
was already used in the last quarter
items.explanation: The third question asks whether the key result actually measures the objective.

items.prompt: Which key result is outside a team's control?
choices: A metric driven only by another team's code
Fewer incidents in its own service
Writing its own runbooks
items.explanation: A team cannot be accountable for what it cannot move.

items.prompt: The runbook key result scored 'partially' on tracing because...
choices: it cannot be written by the team alone
it has no checklist that can be completed
it supports recovery, not reliability
items.explanation: It supports recovery speed rather than measuring reliability directly.

items.prompt: What role does an enabler key result play?
choices: It replaces the objective
It supports another key result
It repeats the incident count again
items.explanation: An enabler makes another key result achievable.

items.prompt: Should a weak score on one question drop the key result automatically?
choices: Yes, always
Only if the team asks
No, weigh it as information
items.explanation: A weak score tells you its role and is not automatic disqualification.

items.prompt: 'Recovery time from 45 to under 15 minutes' is measurable because...
choices: it is a duration logged automatically
it sounds ambitious enough to impress
leadership happens to like the acronym
items.explanation: A logged duration either meets the target or does not.

items.prompt: Which question does 'make the team happier' fail first?
choices: Control: the team owns it fully, so it passes
Trace: it connects upward clearly
Measurable: no number is defined
items.explanation: With no number or checkable list, it fails the first question.

items.prompt: MTTR stands for...
choices: maximum team response rate
mean time to recovery
min time to release
items.explanation: MTTR is the mean time to recovery after an incident.

items.prompt: Total downtime equals...
choices: incidents divided by recovery time taken
incidents plus recovery time per incident
incidents times their recovery time
items.explanation: Downtime is the number of incidents multiplied by how long each takes to recover.

items.prompt: With 8 incidents of 45 minutes each, total downtime is...
choices: 360 minutes
53 minutes
180 minutes
items.explanation: 8 times 45 is 360 minutes.

items.prompt: With 2 incidents of 45 minutes each, total downtime is...
choices: 47 minutes
22 minutes
90 minutes
items.explanation: 2 times 45 is 90 minutes.

items.prompt: With 8 incidents of 15 minutes each, total downtime is...
choices: 240 minutes
120 minutes
60 minutes
items.explanation: 8 times 15 is 120 minutes.

items.prompt: With 2 incidents of 15 minutes each, total downtime is...
choices: 30 minutes
17 minutes
8 minutes
items.explanation: 2 times 15 is 30 minutes.

items.prompt: Why keep both the incident-count and recovery-time key results?
choices: Leadership requires key results in pairs
They measure the same thing twice
They are two levers on one outcome
items.explanation: Each moves total downtime independently, so both matter.

items.prompt: The roughly 130-minute allowance for 99.9% assumes...
choices: a 90-day quarter, 129,600 minutes
a 30-day month with 43,200 minutes
a full 365-day year of 525,600 minutes
items.explanation: 0.1 percent of 129,600 minutes is about 130 minutes.

items.prompt: If incidents fall but recovery stays at 45 minutes, downtime...
choices: is zero automatically once incidents fall
still depends on recovery time
becomes unmeasurable
items.explanation: Downtime is still the product, so recovery time still matters.

items.prompt: A team's goal reads 'Make onboarding smoother.' A teammate says it is fine because everyone knows what it means. What is the strongest objection?
choices: It names no single owner for the onboarding flow
It sets no date, so the work could drift on forever
It has no measurable result to confirm it happened
It is too ambitious for one quarter of work
items.explanation: The core gap is the missing measurable result. Dates and owners help, but without a number, even a finished quarter cannot be judged.
items.reference:
Objective vs. key result
objective: why it matters, qualitative
key result: did it happen, a number
pair: an OKR
Why: an objective gives direction and a key result makes it checkable, so a goal needs both.
items.learnMore:
Objective and key result

An objective says what success looks like in words; key results are the measurable outcomes that show progress toward it. Without key results the objective is a slogan; without the objective the numbers have no purpose.

Common mistake

Treating a vague phrase like 'improve code quality' as if it were already a measurable goal.
items.reflection: Think of a goal you set for yourself that stayed a vague wish. What number would have told you it happened?

items.prompt: Which pairing is a proper objective with a matching key result?
choices: Objective: reduce signup drop-off. Key result: improve the signup page for new users
Objective: ship the redesign. Key result: ship the redesign before the deadline
Objective: reach 70% completion. Key result: make signup painless for every user
Objective: make signup painless. Key result: signup completion rises from 55% to 70%
items.explanation: The objective is qualitative and the key result is a checkable number. The other pairings blur the two or restate the same task. The percentages are illustrative.

items.prompt: Team A picked 'cut checkout failures from 5% to 1%' after asking finance what hurt revenue. Team B picked 'refactor the payments module' because it looked messy. Both finish everything. What can be said?
choices: Both succeeded equally, since both finished
Neither can be judged until next quarter starts
Team B succeeded more, having done harder work
Only Team A is known to have aimed at a need
items.explanation: Finishing proves effort, not aim. Team A derived its goal from a stated need, while Team B's link to any need is unstated. The percentages are illustrative.
items.reference:
Where a goal comes from
company priority: reduce outages hurting renewals
team objective: derived from that need
isolated pick: 'improve code quality', no link
Why: a goal chosen in isolation can be fully achieved and still miss what the organization needed.
items.learnMore:
Cascading goals

Cascading means translating a goal from one level of the organization into the next, so the team's objective contributes to what the level above needs. Ask what the organization needs from the team before asking what to measure.

Common mistake

Assuming a hard-working quarter proves the goal was right.
items.reflection: Pick something you worked hard on recently. Who was it for, and did they agree it was the priority?

Answer every ticket within a single working day

items.explanation: Helping new customers succeed early connects directly to early churn. The others are plausible activities with no stated link.

items.prompt: Which goal fails the second test while passing the first?
choices: Cut P1 incidents from 8 to 2, tied to the company uptime priority
Raise unit-test coverage from 62% to 75%, with no stated need
Improve how reliable the service feels to everyone using it daily
Write incident runbooks to speed up recovery times for the team
items.explanation: The coverage goal has a number but no stated upward link. The first and last tie to a priority, and the third fails the first test. The figures are illustrative.
items.reference:
The two-question test
Q1: what number tells us this happened?
Q2: what does it connect to one level up?
'improve code quality': fails both
Why: a goal can fail either question alone, and only a goal that answers both can be held to account.
items.learnMore:
Two independent tests

Measurability and traceability fail independently. A numbered goal can be pointless, and a well-aimed goal can be unverifiable. Asking both questions every time catches both.

Common mistake

Fixing only one gap, such as adding a number to a goal that was never tied to a need.
items.reflection: Take a goal from any team you know. Can it answer both questions, and which one is harder to answer?

items.prompt: A key result says 'migrate the service to a new queue system', and nobody on the team has operated one. Which plan addresses the gap?
choices: Start the migration early and hope speed teaches the team
Assign it to whoever has the most free time
Add an early spike with expert help, then migrate
Keep the key result and remove the reviews
items.explanation: A short learning step with expert support names the gap and puts the learning into the plan. The others assume effort closes it.
items.reference:
Skill gap analysis
goal needs: runbooks for 10 failure modes
team has: nobody who has written one
plan: pair the first attempt, review it, reuse it
Why: an unnamed gap becomes a delivery risk, and a named gap becomes part of the plan.
items.learnMore:
Naming the gap

A skill gap analysis compares what the team can do today with what the key results require. Doing it before the quarter starts lets the plan include learning, pairing or review instead of assuming effort is enough.

Common mistake

Counting a deliverable as done because it exists, even though nobody could use it under pressure.
items.reflection: Think of a task you accepted without having done it before. What would naming the gap up front have changed?

items.prompt: Which situation is a skill gap and not a capacity gap?

The team has time and has never written a usable runbook
The team has time and also several past runbooks
The team lacks time and also lacks reviewers entirely
items.explanation: A skill gap is about knowing how. The first and last describe too little time, and the third describes no gap at all.

items.learnMore:
Weighing the scores

A weak score on one question is information, not an automatic cut. An enabler key result can score partially on tracing and still earn its place if it supports another key result.

Common mistake

Dropping a useful enabler, or mistaking it for an independent measure of the objective.
items.reflection: Look at a target you are held to. Which of the three questions would it struggle with?

items.prompt: For a reliability objective, a team proposes the key result 'ship three new dashboards'. It is measurable and within control. What is the best verdict?
choices: Keep it as written, since two of three questions pass
Reword it so the dashboards measure reliability
Drop it entirely, since dashboards never help anyone
Keep it unchanged and add a fourth question to it
items.explanation: The weak point is tracing. A dashboard that surfaces failures could connect to reliability, so the fix is to tie it to the objective.
items.reference:
Three questions per key result
measurable: a number or a checkable list
in the team's control: can they move it?
traces to the objective: does it measure it?
Why: a key result that fails a question is still informative, because the weak score says what role it plays.

items.prompt: Which item is an enabler for the recovery-time key result, and not a direct measure of reliability?
choices: Total P1 incidents counted at quarter end
Customer-visible downtime in minutes per quarter
Alerts that page the on-call engineer promptly
Uptime percentage reported to leadership monthly
items.explanation: Prompt, correct paging helps recovery without being a reliability measure itself. The other three measure outcomes directly.

items.prompt: Half of a team's P1 incidents originate in a dependency owned by another team. The key result is 'P1 incidents to 2 or fewer'. What should the manager do?
choices: Keep it as written and ignore the dependency completely
Drop the key result since it is entirely out of reach
Narrow it to its own incidents and flag the rest
Replace it with a key result about team morale levels
items.explanation: Control wobbles for the shared half. Narrowing the key result and flagging the dependency keeps it accountable.

items.prompt: A quarter has 5 P1 incidents of 30 minutes each. Using a 90-day quarter, does 99.9% uptime hold?
choices: Yes, 150 minutes is well within the allowance
No, 150 minutes exceeds roughly 130 minutes
Yes, 35 minutes is within the allowance overall
No, 35 minutes exceeds roughly 130 minutes in total
items.explanation: 5 times 30 is 150 minutes, which is above the allowance of about 130 minutes (0.1% of 129,600).
items.reference:
Downtime = incidents x recovery time
today: 8 x 45 = 360 min
only incidents cut: 2 x 45 = 90 min
only recovery cut: 8 x 15 = 120 min
both: 2 x 15 = 30 min (allowance about 130)
Why: two key results are two independent levers on the same customer-felt outcome, and pulling both leaves a margin.
items.learnMore:
Two levers, one outcome

Customers feel total downtime, which is how many incidents happen times how long each lasts. Assuming a 90-day quarter and counting only P1 downtime, 99.9% uptime allows about 130 minutes.

Common mistake

Treating the second key result as redundant and then missing the target when one lever slips.
items.reflection: Where in your own work does one outcome depend on two multiplied factors, and which one are you tracking?

items.prompt: Starting from 8 incidents of 45 minutes, which single change cuts the most downtime?
choices: Cut incidents from 8 to 4
Cut recovery from 45 to 30 minutes
Cut incidents from 8 to 6
Cut recovery from 45 to 35 minutes
items.explanation: Halving incidents gives 180 minutes, a saving of 180. The other changes save 120, 90 and 80 minutes.

items.prompt: A team is at 8 incidents of 15 minutes each, 120 minutes in total. One extra 15-minute incident happens. What follows?
choices: It stays within the allowance, with about 5 minutes to spare
It stays within the allowance, with about 10 minutes to spare
It breaks the allowance, at 135 minutes against about 130
It breaks the allowance, at 128 minutes against about 130
items.explanation: Nine incidents of 15 minutes is 135 minutes, over about 130. This is why hitting only one key result leaves little margin.

items.prompt: A team halves incidents from 8 to 4 but recovery worsens to 60 minutes. What is the result?
choices: It falls to 240 minutes, still above the allowance
Downtime falls to 120 minutes, within the allowance
Downtime stays at 360 minutes, unchanged
Downtime rises to 480 minutes, worse than today
items.explanation: 4 times 60 is 240 minutes. It beats the 360 baseline but misses 130, showing a single lever is not enough.
